{/* ===================================================== 2. PROJECT OVERVIEW ====================================================== */}
{getSectionTag("02 · PROJECT OVERVIEW")}

What is Volvo Partner Connect 2.0?

Volvo Partner Connect 2.0 is an enterprise B2B platform engineered to streamline commercial vehicle dealership operations, business analytics, service throughput, and compliance across national dealer networks.

Prior to this platform, dealerships and regional directors operated across disconnected tools: static Excel spreadsheets for quarterly Performance Development Plans (PDP), isolated databases for technician competence, and manual PDF dossiers compiled before monthly operational reviews.

My engagement focused on transforming high-density business requirements into intuitive digital workflows, structuring information architecture across 20+ modules, and establishing a unified design system.

MY CORE RESPONSIBILITIES & CONTRIBUTIONS
  • Business Requirements: Deconstructed multi-stakeholder needs and compliance regulations.
  • Information Architecture: Structured 20+ operational modules into a cohesive hierarchy.
  • Dashboard Experience: Designed high-density KPI cards and contextual trend visuals.
  • Tabular Optimization: Engineered dense tables with sticky headers, search, and drawer expansion.
  • Design System: Built scalable component tokens across Figma and CSS variables.
  • Stakeholder Collaboration: Iterated designs with product managers, directors, and developers.
{/* ===================================================== 3. PROBLEM STATEMENT ====================================================== */}
{getSectionTag("03 · PROBLEM STATEMENT")}

Complex business operations need more than disconnected dashboards.

Commercial vehicle networks require seamless coordination between equipment sales, spare parts inventories, facility investments, and technician competence. However, the existing ecosystem suffered from deep systemic friction:

1. Information Complexity

Dense data scattered across 20+ submodules without clear visual prioritization.

2. Organizing Operational Data

Difficulty sorting through thousands of equipment VINs, warranty claims, and parts orders.

3. Inconsistent Patterns

Disjointed filter bars, conflicting table styles, and varying color states across screens.

4. Understanding KPI Trends

Isolated numbers without historical baseline benchmarks or peer percentile comparisons.

5. Fragmented Navigation

Losing active dealership context when jumping between PDP, DFHM audits, and training rosters.

6. Scalability Bottlenecks

Inability to add new product lines (such as electric vehicle battery bays) without redesigning screens.

{/* Visual Problem Diagram */}
{/* ===================================================== 4. BUSINESS GOALS ====================================================== */}
{getSectionTag("04 · STRATEGIC BUSINESS GOALS")}

Designing for operational clarity & scalability

GOAL 01

Discoverability

Ensure regional managers find at-risk dealership metrics within two clicks from login.

GOAL 02

Consistency

Standardize table controls, filter bars, and status tokens across all 20+ submodules.

GOAL 03

Actionable Workflows

Directly bridge diagnostic audit gaps into assigned, SLA-tracked corrective action tickets.

GOAL 04

Component Scalability

Establish atomic Figma components mapping directly to frontend development tokens.

{/* ===================================================== 5. TARGET USERS & PROPOSED PERSONAS ====================================================== */}
{getSectionTag("05 · TARGET USERS & PROPOSED PERSONAS")}

Designed for Multi-Tiered Enterprise Roles

To ensure relevant role-based access control (RBAC), proposed personas were synthesized across strategic, operational, and technical dealership functions.

{/* ===================================================== 6. USER RESEARCH AND DISCOVERY ====================================================== */}
{getSectionTag("06 · DISCOVERY & REQUIREMENTS GATHERING")}

Understanding business requirements before designing interfaces.

In enterprise B2B environments, design begins with rigorous business analysis. Rather than jumping into visual polish, the discovery process centered on deconstructing complex Business Requirement Documents (BRDs), analyzing existing spreadsheet workflows, and auditing legacy data models.

I conducted structured working sessions with Product Managers, Business Analysts, and Technical Leads to map out data dependencies: how a drop in Parts & Lubes inventory correlates with customer turnaround times in the workshop bays.

DOCUMENTED DISCOVERY METHODOLOGY (NO FABRICATED STATS)

[Stakeholder Alignment]: Conducted iterative requirement reviews with OEM product owners.

[Workflow Deconstruction]: Reverse-engineered 15+ legacy Excel tracking templates.

Complex Information Needs Organization

INSIGHT 02

Data Visualization Needs Context

Raw numbers without comparison benchmarks are meaningless. Every metric must show baseline targets and QoQ trend variance.

Solution: Dual-Axis Benchmark Cards
INSIGHT 03

Consistency Breeds Familiarity

Standardizing filter toolbars and status tokens cut cross-module onboarding time for regional managers.

Solution: Shared Component Tokens
INSIGHT 04

Workflows Should Support Action

Dashboards must not stop at passive reporting. Users need a direct path to create corrective tickets and assign ownership.

Solution: Inline Action Planner Integration
INSIGHT 05

Reusable Patterns Ensure Scalability

An atomic design system allowed our team to scale from 8 to 20+ modules without accumulating visual design debt.

Solution: 40+ Atomic UI Component Tokens

Engineering Solutions for Enterprise Constraints

CHALLENGE 01

Complex Data Presentation

Overwhelming raw data tables with 40+ columns causing severe user fatigue.

Solution: Clear KPI hierarchy with progressive side-drawer disclosure.
CHALLENGE 02

Multiple Product Modules

Jumping between PDP, Dealer Investment, and Competence caused loss of active dealer context.

Solution: Persistent global top navigation with preserved session filters.
CHALLENGE 03

Dense Operational Tables

Horizontal scrolling caused users to lose track of which dealership row they were reviewing.

Solution: Sticky primary columns, column visibility toggles, and monospaced tabular numerals.
CHALLENGE 04

Performance Analysis

Static numbers failed to communicate whether a dealership was on track to meet annual goals.

Solution: Dual-axis trend charts with peer percentile comparisons.
CHALLENGE 05

Interface Inconsistency

Disjointed filter bars and button placements created unnecessary learning curves.

Solution: Standardized 40+ atomic component library across all modules.
CHALLENGE 06

Responsive Tablet Use

Field consultants conducting workshop audits required touch-friendly layouts on rugged tablets.

Solution: Touch-target padding (min 44px) and offline-sync audit checklist.

{/* ===================================================== 18. LEARNINGS & RETROSPECTIVE ====================================================== */}
{getSectionTag("18 · LEARNINGS & RETROSPECTIVE")}

Enterprise product design is about making complexity understandable.

1. Deep Domain Empathy Precedes UI Polish

Designing for commercial heavy machinery requires understanding equipment utilization cycles, warranty liability windows, and dealership cash flow. A designer who cannot read an operational balance sheet cannot design an enterprise dashboard.

2. Designing for Multiple Roles Requires Rigorous RBAC

What is vital for a Dealer Principal is noise for a workshop technician. Establishing clear role-based access control (RBAC) was the most critical design decision in reducing cognitive clutter.

3. Frontend Feasibility Must Be Baked In Early

Designing 40-column tables without considering React virtualization or DOM node rendering bottlenecks leads to catastrophic performance drops. Working closely with engineers ensured all designs scrolled at silky 60fps.

4. Personal Reflection as a Product Designer

Working on Volvo Partner Connect 2.0 at Advitiix Technovate reinforced that great enterprise UX is not about superficial aesthetics—it is about synthesizing immense complexity into tools that give professionals mastery over their daily work.
